Adding a cache in front of your database can significantly improve performance, especially if your application experiences high traffic or if database queries are complex and time-consuming. A cache acts as an intermediary layer that stores frequently accessed data, reducing the need to query the database directly. This can lead to faster response times and reduced load on your database server.

Before implementing a cache, consider the following factors:

1. **Cache Invalidation**: Determine a strategy for invalidating cache entries when the underlying data changes. This is crucial to ensure that users always receive the most up-to-date information.

2. **Cache Size**: Consider the appropriate size for your cache. It should be large enough to store frequently accessed data but not so large that it consumes excessive memory resources.

3. **Cache Hit Ratio**: Monitor the cache hit ratio to ensure that your cache is effectively reducing database load. A high hit ratio indicates that the cache is being used efficiently.

4. **Consistency**: Decide on the consistency model that suits your application. Some applications may prefer eventual consistency, while others require strong consistency.

5. **Technology**: Choose a caching solution that fits your infrastructure and development stack. Popular options include Redis, Memcached, and in-memory databases.

If your application can benefit from a cache and you address these considerations, adding a cache in front of your database can be a valuable optimization.

Learning based Malicious Web Sites Detection Malicious Web sites largely promote the growth of Internet criminal activities and constrain the development of Web services. As a result, there has been strong motivation to develop systemic solution to stopping the user from visiting such Web sites. We propose a learning based approach to classifying Web sites into 3 classes: Benign, Spam and Malicious. Our mechanism only analyzes the Uniform Resource Locator (URL) itself without accessing the content of Web sites. Thus, it eliminates the run-time latency and the possibility of exposing users to the browser based vulnerabilities. By employing learning algorithms, our scheme achieves better performance on generality and coverage compared with blacklisting service. URLs of the websites are separated into 3 classes: Given single URL, we extract its features and  categorize them into 3 classes: Lexical features are based on the observation that the URLs of many illegal sites look different, compared with legitimate sites. Analyzing lexical features enables us to capture the property for classification purposes. We first distinguish the two parts of a URL: the host name and the path, from which we extract bag-of-words (strings delimited by ‘/’,  ‘?’, ‘.’, ‘=’,  ‘-’ and  ‘ ’). We find that phishing   website  prefers  to have  longer  URL,  more  levels (delimited by dot), more tokens in domain  and  path, longer token. Besides, phishing and malware websites could pretend to be a benign  one by  containing popular brand names  as tokens other than those in second-level  domain. Considering phishing  websites and malware websites may use IP address directly so as  to cover  the  suspicious  URL,  which  is very rare in benign case. Also, phishing URLs are found to contain several suggestive word tokens(confirm,  account, banking, secure,  ebayisapi, webscr,  login,  signin), we check the presence of these security sensitive words and include the binary value in our features. Intuitively, malicious sites are always less popular than benign ones. For this reason, site popularity can be considered as an important feature. Traffic rank feature is acquired from Alexa.com. Host-based features are based on the observation that malicious sites are always registered in less reputable hosting centers or regions. All of URLs in the dataset are labeled. We used two supervised learning algorithms random forest and support vector machine to train using scikit-learn library.

Lafayette is a system to store various email abuse reports sent in ARF. It is organized in such a way that fraudulent emails can be easily selected, sorted and reported back to the resource owners. For instance it can be used to receive DMARC failure reports. Documentation and Screenshots at This requires python, flask and mysql server. Detecting fraudulent emails is a combination of an automatic process, and a manual one. The DMARC failure reports indicate a non authenticated email, sometimes it is a bounce (people forget to sign their bounces), sometimes it is an auto-reply. So the system tries to classify each email so we can ignore reports of bounces and others. A cursory look of the rest of the failure reports allows to identify patterns. For instance "all emails in the last 2 days with the subject containing 'wire transfer'" or "all emails in the last 2 days which contain an URL that terminates by mail.htm". Once the emails are identified they can be selected to be reported to the abuse email address of the network owner of the original sending IP. Lafayette collects, identifies and reports fraudulent emails, so the zombies get fixed and removed from the botnet they belong to, at the same time the URLs are added in blocking lists that browsers use. For ease of use, a graph of the last few days report indicates visually when there is a potential fraudulent activity going on and a world heat map of reported emails give an indication from which networks fraudulent activity is coming from.
